title: Did Your Paycheck Keep Up? Prices, Wages and Houses Since 2000
description:
In September 2026 US prices jumped, led by fuel, and real pay fell compared with a year earlier. Is this the moment paychecks fell behind, or one bad year in a longer story?

We compare a quarter century of consumer prices, average hourly pay and house prices from official public data, and give our honest take on what it means for your money.

cpi_month_news.label: CPI, September monthly change
cpi_month_news.citation: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for September 2026 (released 14 Oct 2026), as reported by First Trust: consumer prices rose 0.6% in September

real_pay_news.label: Real average hourly earnings, change on a year earlier
real_pay_news.citation: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for September 2026 (released 14 Oct 2026), as reported by First Trust: real average hourly earnings down 0.7% from a year earlier

gas_news.label: Gasoline prices, September monthly change
gas_news.citation: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for September 2026 (released 14 Oct 2026), as reported by First Trust: gasoline prices up 9.1% in September

claims.says: Pay rose faster than prices since 2000
Prices rose much faster in 2021-2023 than the yearly pace before the pandemic
House prices rose faster than both prices and pay
A median home costs more hours of work today than in 2000
Real pay fell over the past year (news report)

scenes.narration: On the fourteenth of October, the government's monthly inflation report landed, and it was not kind to paychecks. Prices rose {{ latest(cpi_month_news) | pct1 }} in September alone. Once you take those higher prices into account, the average worker's pay now buys {{ -latest(real_pay_news) | pct1 }} less than it did a year ago. So is this the moment wages finally fell behind for good? Or is it one bad year in a much longer story? To answer that, we need more than one month of news. We need a quarter of a century of data.

chart.title: Real pay fell over the past year
chart.label: WHAT JUST HAPPENED

scenes.narration: Most of the damage came from one place: the pump. Petrol prices jumped {{ latest(gas_news) | pct1 }} in a single month, and that one item explained more than half of the rise in prices. Fuel is the price people notice most, because they see it on a big sign every time they drive past.

chart.query: gasoline pump price sign United States
chart.caption: Fuel drove September's jump

scenes.narration: In January 2000, the average American production worker earned {{ value(wages, "2000-01") | usd_cents }} an hour. In the latest data, that number is {{ latest(wages) | usd_cents }}. On paper, that is a huge raise. But over the same years, almost everything you buy got more expensive too. Groceries, rent, insurance, a tank of fuel. So here is the question for today. Did your paycheck actually keep up? Instead of guessing, we are going to answer it with the official data, one chart at a time.

Let's start with prices. This line is the consumer price index. Every month, government statisticians check the prices of a huge basket of everyday things, from bread to doctor visits, and combine them into one number. We set it to one hundred in January 2000, so you can read the line as a percentage of what things cost back then. Since January 2000, it has gone up {{ pct_change(cpi, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}. In plain words, a basket of shopping that cost {{ 100 | usd }} in 2000 costs about {{ in_todays_money(100, cpi, "2000-01") | usd }} today.
Think of it as one giant shopping trolley that the whole country fills every month.

chart.caption: The basket behind the price index

scenes.narration: For most of that time, the rise was slow and steady. Before the pandemic, prices grew about {{ cagr(cpi, "2000-01", "2019-12") | pct1 }} a year. That is the kind of inflation you barely notice. Then came the jump. Between January 2021 and January 2023 alone, prices rose {{ pct_change(cpi, "2021-01", "2023-01") | pct }}. Two years did the work of many normal years, and that is why the last few years felt so different at the checkout.

Now let's bring in wages. This is average hourly pay for production and non-supervisory workers, which covers most people who work for a living. Over the same period, it rose {{ pct_change(wages, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}. When we put both lines on the same scale, both starting at one hundred in the year 2000, you can watch the race directly. For years the two lines run close together. Then they separate.

Here are the two totals side by side. Prices are up {{ pct_change(cpi, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}, and pay is up {{ pct_change(wages, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}. So on average, pay is ahead. After adjusting for inflation, an hour of work now buys about {{ ratio(wages, "2000-01", "latest") / ratio(cpi, "2000-01", "latest") - 1 | pct }} more than it did in 2000. That is a real gain. But it is spread over a quarter of a century, so from one year to the next it is easy to miss, especially when a few bad years eat into it.
And then there is the biggest purchase most people ever make.

chart.caption: The biggest purchase most people make

scenes.narration: Houses are a different story. The Case-Shiller index follows the price of the same homes as they are sold again and again, so it measures how much the same house has gained in value. Since January 2000, it has risen {{ pct_change(homes, "2000-01", "latest") | pct }}. You can see the bubble before 2008, the crash, and then a long climb that left both prices and wages far behind.

Let's make that personal. The median price of a new home sold in the United States went from {{ value(median_home, "2000-03") | usd }} in early 2000 to {{ latest(median_home) | usd }} in the latest data. Now divide that by the average hourly wage. In 2000, the median home cost about {{ value(median_home, "2000-03") / value(wages, "2000-03") | num }} hours of work. Today it costs about {{ latest(median_home) / latest(wages) | num }} hours. Same kind of house, a lot more of your life spent paying for it.

chart.title: Hours of work to buy the median new home
chart.subtitle: Median sales price divided by average hourly pay

scenes.narration: Here is my take. The latest month is a real warning, because a fuel shock hits people who drive to work hardest, and pay rarely adjusts within a year. But one bad year does not erase twenty-five years of slow gains in what an hour of work buys. The bigger problem is housing. That gap built up over two decades, and no single good month for wages will close it. What would change my mind? If real pay keeps falling for another year after fuel prices calm down, that would point to something deeper than a price spike. These are national averages, so your own city, job and rent can look very different. But next time someone says wages never keep up, you will know where to look.

chart.title: One bad year, one long housing problem
chart.label: MY TAKE

method: We rebase prices, hourly pay and house prices to 100 in January 2000 so they can share one chart, and compare the median new-home price with hourly pay to count the hours of work a home costs.

references.says: September CPI up 0.6% (3.7% on a year earlier), gasoline up 9.1%, real average hourly earnings down 0.5% in the month and 0.7% on a year earlier, citing the BLS release

short.title: House prices left paychecks far behind
